description_full: Elbit Systems Ltd., together with its subsidiaries, develops and supplies defense and homeland security arenas products and services in Israel, North America, Europe, the Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and internationally. The company operates through five segments: Aerospace; C4I and Cyber; Intelligence, Surveillance, Target Acquisition and Reconnaissance and Electronic Warfare; Land; and Elbit Systems of America. It offers airborne platforms, unmanned aerial solutions, precision guided munition sensors, aerostructures, training and simulator systems, flight academy solutions, and commercial aviation systems; and command, control, communications, computer, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance systems, as well as data links and radio communication systems and equipment, cyber intelligence solutions, and autonomous and homeland security solutions. The company also provides various electro-optic laser solutions and countermeasure systems and products, naval combat management and sonar systems, and electronic warfare, signal Intelligence, and radar systems; indirect fire, turrets and weapons, ammunition and munition, and active protection systems; and products, system solutions, and support services to defense, homeland security, law enforcement, commercial aviation, and medical instrumentation markets. It serves various governments and companies. The company was incorporated in 1966 and is based in Haifa, Israel.

financial_summary: Elbit Systems Ltd. is a large-cap industrials business with a $32.1B market cap on $7.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 7% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 26%.

The business throws off $553M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.46× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 4.6×.

Net dilution runs at 1.4% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insiders hold 41% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 8% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.76x).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 69% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 33% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 47% and a beta of 0.48, it is more defensive than the market.
About $54.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 29% in the 2020 crash, 33% in the 2022 bear market and 42% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $337 (margin of safety -104%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $157 to $796 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 48.3 vs 23.1, EV/EBITDA 30.4 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 58.1 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 145% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $837 on average, 22% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 7.2%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.18).
It runs a 26% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.46x.
ROE of 13% is amplified by 3.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 7.6% of revenue on R&D and 0.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $533.7M (2% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.6, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 252 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.9% over 3 years, 11.2% over 5 years and 9.8% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 12.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 30.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.69 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 3.5x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 22%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 2.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 41.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 27%.
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-1.4%), diluting holders.
The share count has grown 1.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 28 consecutive years, raising it 7.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 21,000 employees, each generates about $378K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 8.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $26K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.1M (8x revenue per employee).
